p.s: On August twenty sixth, twenty twenty six, a glacier collapsed on the Nepal-Tibet border.
The debris flow that followed killed over six hundred people, with thousands still missing.
It hit with enough force to register on seismographs, as if it were its own earthquake.
Not local authorities, not the institutions with dedicated instrumentation nearby.

And this wasn't a first. India has already lived through two close relatives of this same disaster: Chamoli, in twenty twenty-one, and South Lhonak Lake in Sikkim, in twenty twenty-three — a lake that had been formally flagged as dangerous four years before it finally broke, and still killed forty-two people.
Here's the part that doesn't make headlines. India's disaster management authority actively monitors fifty-six glacial lakes.
There are over twenty-eight thousand catalogued across the Indian Himalayan region alone.
Nobody can predict which one fails next. But almost nobody is even watching most of them.
This is GlacierWatch.

It's built for state disaster management authorities, and for village-level disaster committees in Himalayan districts — the people who have to decide, this week, with limited field teams and limited time, which sites deserve a closer look.
It is not built to replace the glaciologists and geotechnical engineers who make the real, on-the-ground call.
And here's the choice we made on purpose: GlacierWatch does not predict avalanches or glacial lake outburst floods. It never will.
A tool that claimed to know when the next one hits would be dishonest — and worse, it could talk someone out of evacuating when they shouldn't be.
What we built instead is narrower, and honest: triage.
Take what's already documented and published about a hazard site. Combine it with this week's real, observed weather and seismic conditions.
And tell a human, plainly, which sites deserve attention right now — and which don't.
Let's watch it run.

This is the live app. Notice the banner at the top, before anything else loads: this is decision support, not a prediction system. That disclaimer is on every single report GlacierWatch ever produces.

We click Run GlacierWatch. No file to upload, no form to fill in — it runs against a small, bundled watchlist of four real Himalayan sites, and every fact about them is sourced to a published assessment.

Watch the activity log. This is a Strands agent orchestrator, and every one of these lines is a real tool call, happening live: loading the watchlist, then reaching out to Open-Meteo for today's real rainfall data, and to the U.S. Geological Survey for real recent earthquake activity near each site.
Nothing here is mocked. If a fetch fails, the agent says so, instead of quietly making up a number.
Once it finishes, this is the Weekly Watchlist — the trusted report.

Two of our four sites, Gepang Gath and Samudra Tapu in Himachal Pradesh, come back elevated: both have a documented, formally assessed high-risk profile, but this week's real conditions show no acute trigger — no extreme rainfall, no significant nearby seismic activity.
The other two sites are historical case studies, already drained, held at routine — used only to calibrate the tool's rainfall threshold, never implied to be building toward another failure.

And here's Current Conditions — the actual live numbers behind that judgment: today's precipitation, categorized on India's own official rainfall scale, and the nearest recent seismic events, with their distance and magnitude spelled out.
Every number here is real, fetched at the moment this report ran.
That's GlacierWatch: published, cited hazard data, plus this week's real conditions, turned into one honest, disclaimed priority list.
What's next is scale. The watchlist today is four sites. India's monitoring list is fifty-six. The full catalogue is over twenty-eight thousand.
As that data becomes available in usable form, GlacierWatch is built to grow into it — without ever growing into a promise it can't keep.
Because the honest answer to "can you predict the next glacier disaster" is no.
But "can you help someone watch the right place this week" — that one, we can actually say yes to.
